To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
antibiotic resistance has increased in the last years in respiratory tract pathogens.
the prevalence of antimicrobial resistance in respiratory tract pathogens is high, and that the use of antibiotics should be guided by local resistance data.

In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
antibiotic therapy is not always necessary and should be used only when the patient is symptomatic.
antibiotic therapy should be used in the treatment of community-acquired pneumonia, acute exacerbation of chronic bronchitis, and in severe infections caused by Haemophilus or Moraxella.

the use of antibiotics in respiratory tract infection is indicated when: (a) the clinical picture is suggestive of an infection; (b) there is evidence of a bacterial infection, such as positive cultures or Gram staining of the sputum; (c) there is no response to symptomatic treatment; and (d) the infection is severe.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
in the treatment of acute exacerbations of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, the first choice should be a third-generation cephalosporin.

the use of antibiotics for respiratory tract infections should be restricted to the most severe infections, namely pneumonia, exacerbations of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), and infections in immunocompromised patients, and to infections in which there is no other choice of therapy.
the antibiotic therapy for respiratory tract infections should be based on the clinical presentation of the patient and the local resistance pattern.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the use of antibiotic therapy for respiratory tract infections should be based on clinical judgment and not on the results of microbiological tests.
the antibiotic treatment should be restricted to patients who have severe or complicated infections.
in patients with acute bronchitis and uncomplicated community-acquired pneumonia, the empirical treatment should be based on local resistance patterns of the most common pathogens.
